title: How Soylent Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Soylent, the meal replacement drink born from software engineer Rob Brian Hart's 2013 blog post "How I Stopped Eating Food," its Kickstarter success, FDA classification as a food, and its evolution through versions up to 1.7 and Soylent 2.0. They cover the name's link to the novel Make Room! Make Room! rather than the film Soylent Green, the bland taste and flavor add-ins, nutritional profile and essential vs. non-essential nutrients, the 2015 algal flour recall that suspended version 1.6 and its bar, the switch to algal oil from bioreactors, dietitian skepticism, the chewing and blood-glucose point, and a listener email from a expecting mother about breastfeeding episodes.
topics: How I Stopped Eating Food blog

segments.title: Opening banter and Jazz Jeff tangent
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with jokes about DJ Jazzy Jeff, Will Smith, and a fast food joke, then introduce Soylent as a revolutionary product and note that the hosts have not tried it and have no financial interest in it.

segments.title: What Soylent is and its taste
segments.summary: The hosts describe Soylent as a liquid food replacement or meal replacement, likened to pancake batter or cream of wheat, designed to be bland so people do not tire of it and can add their own flavors.

segments.title: Rob Brian Hart and the origins of Soylent
segments.summary: Rob Brian Hart, a software engineer in San Francisco, wanted to cut the time and money spent on eating and the health concerns of his diet, so he researched nutrition and conceived of delivering just the nutrients. The hosts compare it to other meal replacement drinks like Ensure, Slim-Fast and protein shakes.

segments.title: How I Stopped Eating Food blog and the name Soylent
segments.summary: Hart's 2013 blog post 'How I Stopped Eating Food' went viral, reporting weight loss, better performance, lower grocery costs and five minutes a day of preparation. The hosts discuss the name Soylent, its link to the novel Make Room! Make Room! by Harry Harrison rather than the film Soylent Green, and the spoiler of that film's ending.

segments.title: Kickstarter, FDA classification and rapid growth
segments.summary: Hart raised about three million dollars on Kickstarter, the FDA classified Soylent as a food rather than a dietary supplement, and manufacturing went to Rosa Labs in Los Angeles. Sales reached about thirty thousand units a month by 2014, within seven months of first shipments in May 2014. DIY Soylent subculture is also mentioned.

segments.title: Shelf life, emergency food, and Soylent versions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the idea of keeping Soylent as emergency food, the year-long shelf life of sealed packets, and the company's walk-back from claims that people could live only on Soylent. They note version 1.7 and the new Soylent 2.0 ready-to-drink line, including a caffeinated bottle.

segments.title: Ingredient changes, algal flour recall and nutrition facts
segments.summary: Version 1.6 was suspended after algal flour caused violent illness, which also took the Soylent bar off the market. Version 1.7 replaced fish oil with algal oil from bioreactors for vegan and environmental reasons. The hosts review the main ingredients (soy protein, algal oil, maltodextrin, canola oil) and the nutrition facts, including the vitamins and essential nutrients and the absence of non-essential nutrients like cholesterol.

segments.title: Taste reviews, dietitian views, and the chewing debate
segments.summary: Taste reactions range from neutral to unpleasant, with Joe Randazza calling it devil's chalk and Lizzie Widdicombe's New Yorker article describing trying it. The hosts discuss the loss of communal eating, the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics spokesperson's skepticism and lack of long-term studies, the one-size-fits-all approach, and a Japanese study on chewing and blood glucose. They also mention Angus Barbieri's long fast.

segments.title: Listener mail on breastfeeding episodes
segments.summary: A listener who is pregnant writes that the two-part breastfeeding episodes matched her childbirth class, and that a supportive partner matters. The hosts thank listeners and invite contact.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck sign off, giving contact information and directing listeners to HowStuffWorks.com.
